# Evidence hierarchy â€” how much to trust a source

Use this to weight sources when synthesizing. Higher tiers dominate lower ones
when they conflict. Always weight by **methodological quality within a tier**,
not tier alone â€” a large, pre-registered RCT can outweigh a weak meta-analysis
of poor studies.

## Tiers (strongest â†’ weakest)

1. **Systematic reviews & meta-analyses** of high-quality studies (Cochrane,
   Campbell, well-conducted PRISMA reviews). Living systematic reviews and
   umbrella reviews sit here too.
2. **Consensus statements from authoritative scientific bodies** â€” WHO, IPCC,
   national academies of science, major professional societies, government
   statistical agencies. These represent expert-aggregated consensus.
3. **Randomized controlled trials (RCTs)** and, in non-clinical fields,
   pre-registered controlled experiments with adequate power.
4. **Quasi-experimental & cohort studies**, natural experiments, large
   longitudinal observational studies.
5. **Case-control and cross-sectional studies**, smaller observational work.
6. **Case reports, case series, mechanistic/animal/in-vitro studies** â€”
   hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory.
7. **Expert opinion, narrative reviews, editorials, textbooks** â€” useful for
   background and framing, weak for specific factual claims.
8. **Preprints** (arXiv, bioRxiv, medRxiv, SSRN) â€” not yet peer-reviewed. Cite
   with an explicit "preprint, not peer-reviewed" flag; upgrade the claim once a
   peer-reviewed version exists.

## Quality signals to check inside any tier

- **Replication**: has the finding been independently reproduced? A single
  striking result is provisional.
- **Sample size & power**; pre-registration; conflicts of interest / funding
  source; effect size and confidence intervals (not just p-values).
- **Recency vs. landmark status**: prefer current evidence, but recognise
  foundational work a field still relies on.
- **Retraction status**: check the source has not been retracted or issued a
  correction (Retraction Watch / Crossref).
- **Citations in context**: highly-cited â‰  correct; look at *how* it is cited
  (supported, disputed, superseded).

## GRADE-style summary language

When stating confidence, use calibrated wording:
- **High certainty** â€” consistent high-quality evidence; consensus.
- **Moderate certainty** â€” generally consistent but with limitations.
- **Low certainty** â€” sparse, conflicting, or low-quality evidence.
- **Very low / contested** â€” active scientific debate; state both sides.
########## CITATION
# Citation standards

Default style for this repository: **APA 7th edition**. Switch on request to
Vancouver (biomedicine), IEEE (engineering/CS), Chicago, or MLA â€” keep one style
consistent within a document.

## Every citation must carry

- Authors, year, title, venue (journal/conference/publisher), volume/issue/pages
  where applicable, and a **resolvable DOI** (or stable URL / arXiv ID).
- For preprints: the server + ID and an explicit **"preprint, not peer-reviewed"**
  note.

## APA 7 quick patterns

- **Journal article**: Author, A. A., & Author, B. B. (Year). Title of article.
  *Journal Name, Volume*(Issue), pages. https://doi.org/xxxxx
- **Book**: Author, A. A. (Year). *Title of work*. Publisher.
- **Report / body**: Organization. (Year). *Title of report* (Report No. if any).
  Publisher/URL.
- **In-text**: (Author, Year) or Author (Year); direct quote adds a page/locator.

## Anti-fabrication rules

1. Do not invent DOIs, page numbers, or author lists. If a field is unknown,
   leave it blank and flag it â€” never guess.
2. Confirm each DOI resolves (Crossref) before including it.
3. Match the in-text claim to the specific passage in the source; note the
   section/page you relied on.
4. If a claimed source cannot be located in any database, remove the claim or
   mark it `UNVERIFIED â€” no retrievable source`.

# Reproducibility pack â€” search logs, PRISMA, retraction & citation audit, BibTeX Concrete formats and checks so a review can be re-run and trusted. ## 1. Machine-readable search log Save alongside each review as `research/-searchlog.yaml`: ```yaml question: "" date_run: 2026-07-23 databases: - name: PubMed query: '("intervention"[tiab] AND "outcome"[tiab]) AND 2015:2026[dp]' hits: 214 kept_after_screen: 18 - name: OpenAlex query: "intervention outcome, type:review, from_publication_date:2015-01-01" hits: 96 kept_after_screen: 11 inclusion: ["systematic reviews", "RCTs", "human", "English/Polish", "2015-2026"] exclusion: ["preprints for final claims", "case reports", "non-scholarly"] counts: { identified: 310, deduplicated: 271, screened: 271, full_text: 44, included: 29 } ``` ## 2. PRISMA flow diagram (mermaid) Embed in systematic reviews; fill the counts from the log above: ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Records identified
n = 310] --> B[After duplicates removed
n = 271] B --> C[Records screened
n = 271] C -->|Excluded n = 227| D[Full-text assessed
n = 44] D -->|Excluded n = 15
with reasons| E[Studies included
n = 29] ``` ## 3. Retraction & correction check (do before citing) For each source with a DOI: 1. Resolve it via Crossref (`mcp__paper-search__get_crossref_paper_by_doi` or `search_crossref`). Confirm authors/year/title/venue match. 2. Inspect Crossref metadata for an `update-to` / relation of type *"is-retracted-by"*, *"has-correction"*, or a title prefixed `RETRACTED:` / `EXPRESSION OF CONCERN`. 3. Cross-check the DOI/title against **Retraction Watch** (scholarly WebSearch). 4. If retracted: do **not** cite as valid evidence â€” cite only when discussing the retraction itself, and drop any claim that depended on it. ## 4. Citation â†” claim audit Before finalising, for every in-text citation confirm all four: - [ ] **Exists** â€” resolvable DOI/record, metadata matches. - [ ] **Supports** â€” the specific passage backs the exact claim (not just the title/topic). - [ ] **Scope** â€” no overreach (correlationâ‰ causation, sample/population fits, single study/preprint not stated as settled). - [ ] **Live** â€” not retracted; still current or explicitly flagged as historical. Record failures as `DROPPED` or `DOWNGRADED` with a reason; never leave a mismatched citation in place. ## 5. BibTeX / Zotero export Emit `research/.bib` for reuse. One verified entry per cited source: ```bibtex @article{key2023, author = {Family, Given and Family2, Given2}, title = {Exact title}, journal = {Journal Name}, year = {2023}, volume = {12}, number = {3}, pages = {45--67}, doi = {10.xxxx/xxxxx} } ``` Only include entries whose DOI resolved in step 3. Flag preprints with `note = {Preprint, not peer-reviewed}`. ########## DOMAINS-CS # Domain pack â€” computer science, ML/AI & engineering ## Sources & databases - **arXiv** (cs.*), **DBLP**, **ACL Anthology**, **IEEE Xplore**, **ACM Digital Library**, **Semantic Scholar**, **OpenReview** (peer reviews are public). - Venues carry weight: top conferences (**NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, ACL, CVPR, OSDI, SIGCOMM, POPL**, â€¦) are the field's peer-reviewed record â€” often more than journals. Check acceptance vs. workshop/non-archival tracks. ## Field specifics - **arXiv is preprint-first.** Flag "not peer-reviewed" unless a peer-reviewed (conference/journal) version exists; prefer the published version and note the venue. - Value **reproducibility artifacts**: code, datasets, model cards, and **artifact-evaluation / reproducibility badges**. A result without runnable code or a benchmark others can reproduce is weaker. - For empirical ML claims: check **baselines, ablations, seeds/variance, compute**, dataset contamination/leakage, and whether the benchmark actually measures the claimed capability. Beware **SOTA-chasing** on a single metric. ## Red flags specific to the field - **Benchmark hacking / overfitting to the test set**, cherry-picked baselines, no error bars, non-reproducible "SOTA", undisclosed hyperparameter tuning. - Vendor/marketing "research" and product blogs presented as evidence (treat as `OBJECT-OF-STUDY`); demo-driven claims without evaluation. - Citation of a withdrawn/updated arXiv version; benchmark leaderboards without peer review. ## Consensus & framing Fewer formal "consensus bodies"; rely on **surveys/systematic reviews**, reproduced results across independent groups, and standards bodies (**IETF, W3C, ISO/IEC, NIST**) where relevant. State that a claim is "an active research area" when reproduction is thin.
